packs.title: Exhibits, libraries and park paths
packs.promise: Compare actual exhibits, make original pages and notice public places in detail.

q.s: Connect two exhibited themes, then make a small idea of your own.
st: Enter the actually opened Leadership Hall on Old Main’s entry level. Choose two currently available sections from Pioneering Women, Texas Women in Politics, the Civics Learning Center or women’s suffrage.
In your own words, record one idea from each section and one difference between the themes. Do not copy a quotation, biography, photograph or speech.

On your own page, invent a small civic-learning activity that responds to that difference. Give it a purpose and two practical steps; it is your proposal, not an endorsement or a statement by someone in the exhibit.
Keep the two source-theme notes and your original activity together. Finish after exit if needed; performing, filming or using a public figure’s voice is unnecessary.

q.s: Collect how a dry path connects land, water and a public park.
st: Use an open public path near a lake. Stay on dry land and choose one short observation area without crossing sports play or blocking the path.

Record three relationships you can actually see: one between path and water, one between path and planted or open land, and one between two routes or edges. Describe forms and directions rather than guessing ecological processes.
Compare two of your records: which relationship is easiest to understand from this position, and which remains uncertain?
Keep three observations and the comparison. No wildlife sighting, full circuit or photo is required.

q.s: Compare one trail detail on the way out and on the way back.
st: At Collins Gate, check actual trail notices and use the open Prairie Trail near the visitor center. Record your start position using an ordinary visible path feature; do not enter the Center.
Follow that same hiking trail for up to three minutes at an easy pace, turning earlier if conditions or visibility call for it. Choose one visible trail-edge detail without leaving the path.
Return along the same path to your start. Compare the detail or its setting from the opposite direction; no fixed bend, sign or wildlife encounter is promised.
Write the start cue, actual outward time and a before/return comparison. Use the remaining time for notes and rest; this is a bounded return, not the reserve’s outer circuit.

packs.title: Denton’s square and nearby public places
packs.promise: Two afternoons of museum evidence, public buildings and a bounded trail walk.

q.s: Collect how actual displays connect objects and local history.
st: Enter the actually opened museum and select three available public exhibit items or interpreted features. No particular case, upstairs room or temporary exhibition is required.
For each, describe one visible detail and paraphrase one historical connection supplied by its interpretation. Mark any uncertainty rather than filling it with a guess.
Compare two records: how do the displayed items provide different kinds of evidence? Keep observation separate from the museum’s account.
Finish three item records and a comparison, after exit if needed. No copying documents, portraits or extended labels.

q.t: An original page after a gallery
q.s: Compare two available works, then make something that belongs to you.
st: Enter the actually opened general-admission gallery scope. Choose two works available to ordinary visitors; if a gallery has a separate charge, use another sufficient opened general-admission gallery or return.
For each work, write one observation about material, arrangement or composition in your own words. Follow the gallery rules; no photography, tracing or artwork reproduction is needed.

After leaving the displays, make a small original page using a general contrast you noticed, such as dense/sparse or curved/straight. Invent your own forms and give the page a one-sentence explanation.
Keep the two observations and original response. No copied subject, signature, title treatment or artist’s voice.

q.s: Walk a short public segment and compare the return view.
st: Use the designated public approach and lawful crossing to reach the A-train Rail Trail south of Sycamore. Choose a start cue on the trail, safely clear of the road and any railway crossing.
Walk south on the open public trail for up to three minutes at an easy pace, turning earlier if conditions require. Choose one actual trail-edge or corridor feature without leaving the public path.
Return along the same trail to the start. Write how your view of the feature or corridor changed with direction; no particular sign, train or fixed turnaround object is promised.
Keep your start cue, actual outward time and an outward/return comparison. Remain on the path; the customer-center information task is separate.
